ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by Mulago Hospital Research Ethics Committee (2349) and the Rutgers University Institutional Review Board (Pro2020003026).
It was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
POCUS-TB participants were enrolled between July 2023 and March 2025 at TBRU/Halting TB enrollment sites and Kampala Capital City Authority health facilities.

Eligible participants were individuals aged 13 years or older who (i) had laboratory-confirmed pulmonary TB (ii) were household contacts (HHCs) of an individual with confirmed pulmonary TB, or (iii) were evaluated fo TB and diagnosed with another respiratory condition.
Index cases were enrolled consecutively from parentstudy participants who met eligibility criteria.
Adult participants provided written informed consent.
Participants recruited from clinic patients undergoing TB evaluation who were diagnosed with another respiratory condition underwent
TB-negative participants were classified by clinician diagnosis as having no respiratory condition (NRC) or another, non-TB respiratory condition (ORC).
For modeling, NRC and ORC participants were combined as TB-negative (TB-).
Participants were randomly allocated at the participant level to training (n = 223, 70.6%), validation (n = 20, 6.3%), and held-out test (n = 73, 23.1%) sets.
Two NRC participants were excluded because no LUS zones were recorded.
Compared with TB-participants, TB+ participants had lower median BMI (19.4 vs 22.4 kg/m²), longer cough duration (12 vs 2 weeks), and longer weight-loss duration (4 vs 0 weeks).
Two participants were excluded, and the remaining 316 were divided into training, validation, and test sets.
Second, TB+ participants were mostly index cases, whereas TB-participants were household contacts or clinic patients.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading driver of morbidity and mortality in low-and middle-income countries.

TB burden is concentrated among people living with HIV and undernutrition, and diagnostic gaps are widest in settings without consistent access to radiography, microbiological testing, or trained radiologists (1).
text.formatted: TB burden is concentrated among people living with HIV and undernutrition, and diagnostic gaps are widest in settings without consistent access to radiography, microbiological testing, or trained radiologists <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Chest radiography is widely used for TB screening and triage (2).
text.formatted: Chest radiography is widely used for TB screening and triage <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref>.

text.text: Its deployment, however, is constrained by equipment cost, maintenance, radiation exposure, and infrastructure (3).
text.formatted: Its deployment, however, is constrained by equipment cost, maintenance, radiation exposure, and infrastructure <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: Point-of-care lung ultrasound (POCUS; LUS) is portable, inexpensive, and radiation-free, and can be acquired at the bedside by trained non-radiologist operators (3, 4).
text.formatted: Point-of-care lung ultrasound (POCUS; LUS) is portable, inexpensive, and radiation-free, and can be acquired at the bedside by trained non-radiologist operators <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4)</ref>.

text.text: However, sonographic findings in pulmonary TB, such as subpleural nodules, consolidation, and B-lines, are not specific to TB, and no standardized criteria exist for interpreting them (3).
text.formatted: However, sonographic findings in pulmonary TB, such as subpleural nodules, consolidation, and B-lines, are not specific to TB, and no standardized criteria exist for interpreting them <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: Emerging proof-of-concept studies to date have evaluated artificial intelligence (AI)assisted LUS for TB.

In a prospective study of 504 symptomatic adults in urban Benin, an ensemble of deep learning models achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.93, with 93% sensitivity and 81% specificity (5).
text.formatted: In a prospective study of 504 symptomatic adults in urban Benin, an ensemble of deep learning models achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.93, with 93% sensitivity and 81% specificity <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: A second model, a convolutional neural network with long short-term memory layers trained on video clips from 497 Zambian participants to detect radiographer-labeled lung abnormalities, achieved AUCs of 0.89-0.92 against a composite TB reference standard (6).
text.formatted: A second model, a convolutional neural network with long short-term memory layers trained on video clips from 497 Zambian participants to detect radiographer-labeled lung abnormalities, achieved AUCs of 0.89-0.92 against a composite TB reference standard <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: We developed SCAN-TB (Sonographic and Clinical AI-guided Navigator for TB triage) which builds on these advances in three ways.

First, we trained models directly on participant-level microbiological TB status using attention-based multiple-instance learning, which treats all lung-zone images from a participant as one diagnostic unit and estimates each zone's contribution.
Second, we used zone-level attention to derive a 6-zone protocol as a shorter alternative to a full 12-zone acquisition.
Third, we hypothesized that combining lung ultrasound with routinely collected clinical variables would discriminate TB better than either source alone.
Here we report model development and internal evaluation in an urban Ugandan cohort.
II.
METHODS Study design and participants.
We conducted a prospective observational sub-study within the Bacterial an Host Determinants in TB Transmission project (TBRU/Halting TB) in Kampala, Uganda.
POCUS-TB participants were enrolled between July 2023 and March 2025 at TBRU/Halting TB enrollment sites and Kampala Capital City Authority health facilities.
The study is reported according to the TRIPOD+AI (7) and study workflow is summarized in Figure 1.

Eligible participants were individuals aged 13 years or older who (i) had laboratory-confirmed pulmonary TB (ii) were household contacts (HHCs) of an individual with confirmed pulmonary TB, or (iii) were evaluated fo TB and diagnosed with another respiratory condition.
Index cases were enrolled consecutively from parentstudy participants who met eligibility criteria.

Reference standard and participant classification.
Pulmonary TB status was based on microbiologic detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum.
Index cases and household contacts underwent both Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra (Ultra) and Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube (MGIT) culture.

Participants with an Ultra-or culture-positive result were classified as TB-positive (TB+).
TB-negative participants were classified by clinician diagnosis as having no respiratory condition (NRC) or another, non-TB respiratory condition (ORC).
For modeling, NRC and ORC participants were combined as TB-negative (TB-).
All participants underwent a standardized LUS examination with a Philips Lumify phased-array probe (Philips Healthcare) connected to an Android tablet.

In this prospective Ugandan cohort, attention-based deep learning of a single still frame per lung zone discriminated microbiologically confirmed pulmonary TB, with test-set AUCs of 0.91-0.95.

Models integrating LUS with routine clinical variables demonstrated high discrimination under both acquisition protocols, although differences in performance across models were not statistically significant.

Point estimates for the combined models, including the streamlined 6-zone model using half the standard acquisition zones, exceeded the 2025 WHO minimum targets for a high-sensitivity screening test in a two-step algorithm (≥90% sensitivity, ≥60% specificity) (25) and the 2014 triage target (≥90% sensitivity at ≥70% specificity) (24).

text.text: However, confidence intervals were wide, and their lower bounds fell below these targets for all models, so attainment remains to be confirmed with prespecified thresholds in larger cohorts.
In illustrative cases, the zones the model weighted most heavily coincided with pathologic findings, and integrated-gradient maps localized these findings within individual images.
Together, these findings suggest that SCAN-TB is a promising portable, radiation-free, sputum-independent triage approach requiring validation in larger studies.

This study adds to emerging evidence of strong AI-assisted LUS performance for TB triage, including direct TB prediction from selected images acquired through a 14-point sliding-scan protocol (5) and abnormality detection from streamlined ultrasound sweeps (6).

text.text: We additionally performed participant-level TB classification across anatomically defined lung zones, directly compared clinical-only, ultrasound-only, and combined models, and included both symptomatic patients and household contacts, a target population for active case finding.

We also explored an abbreviated 6-zone protocol selected using attention weights that retained discrimination, although the modest differences in weights do not definitely establish the optimal zone selection.
The selected zones were all superior zones (anterior, lateral, and posterior), consistent with the upper-lobe predominance of pulmonary TB.
This targeted approach may complement sweep-based protocols by standardizing regional sampling, although prospective comparison is needed to determine the relative efficiency and robustness of each.
The added value of combining imaging with clinical data is clinically plausible.

LUS captures peripheral and pleural manifestations of pulmonary disease, whereas cough duration, weight loss, BMI, and general appearance reflect systemic disease and TB risk that ultrasound alone may not capture.

Because these variables may be routinely collected during screening, integrating them adds little acquisition burden and may help distinguish TB from other conditions with overlapping sonographic findings.
However, AUC differences between models were small (Table S8).

text.text: The strong clinical-only performance likely reflects case mix, because TB-negative participants included asymptomatic household contacts who differed from TB+ participants largely in symptom duration.
This study has limitations to address before clinical implementation.
First, models were developed and internally evaluated in a single Ugandan setting with one ultrasound device and trained operators.
External validation across geographically and epidemiologically distinct cohorts, ultrasound platforms, operator groups, and patient populations will establish generalizability.

Prospective implementation studies with intended end users, including non-specialist operators, should quantify acquisition failure rates, inter-operator variability, usability, and downstream effects on confirmatory testing and time to diagnosis.
Second, TB+ participants were mostly index cases, whereas TB-participants were household contacts or clinic patients.
This enrichment may overestimate performance in active case-finding populations, and with only four TB+ household contacts, none asymptomatic, performance in subclinical TB could not be assessed.

Differences in clinical variable recording, completeness, and microbiological verification (Ultra alone versus Ultra plus culture) across recruitment groups may also introduce recruitment-related confounding and bias.
Third, the test and validation sets were small and derived from a single random split.

This precluded precise estimates across clinically important subgroups such as sex, HIV status, prior TB, disease severity, and smear status, as well as calibration, decision-curve, and net-benefit analyses.
Consequently, whether the model performs equitably across these groups remains to be established.
Fourth, a prespecified single-frame rule provides a standardized, reproducible input, but it omits temporal information such as respiratory dynamics and probe repositioning.

Models using the middle frame remained discriminative but had lower AUCs than those using the first frame (0.85 vs 0.93 for ultrasound-only; 0.90 vs 0.95 for combined), indicating that performance varies by frame choice.
Finally, performance was evaluated under a standardized research protocol and may differ in routine practice.

At the same time, several strengths -including prospective design, microbiologically defined TB status, blinded and standardized LUS acquisition, participant-level separation of training and test data, and direct comparison of full and streamlined acquisition protocols -provide a foundation for future validation.

Our clinically integrated deep learning framework for LUS showed promising internal performance for pulmonary TB triage, and a streamlined 6-zone acquisition protocol may enhance its feasibility at the point of care.

If validated externally, this portable, radiation-free, sputum-independent approach could expand access to TB active case finding and improve targeting of confirmatory testing in resource-constrained settings.
